titleText.es: Unos dicen que el mundo acabará con fuego; otros dicen que con segfaults.
titleText.en: Some say the world will end in fire; some say in segfaults.
titleText.noteEn: A segfault, short for segmentation fault, is a program crash caused by invalid memory access. The line replaces the ice in Robert Frost's poem with a programming failure.

applications.explanationEn: Ahora sets the current time, and que links it to the situation stated next.
A marks the following defined group of people as the direct object of entiendo; los que infieren PERL is the complete group phrase.
A is the linking preposition, and los que identifies an unnamed plural group through the description that follows.
Temo expresses fear, que introduces the feared event, and venere changes from venera to the subjunctive form because the event is presented through that fear.

regions.labelEs: Y SI ALGUNA VEZ LO REESCRIBIERE ESTE SERÍA FINITO Y CON UN PARÉNTESIS DE CIERRE.

applications.explanationEn: Alguna vez supplies an unspecified occasion inside the condition.
Si introduces a condition, and reescribiere is the rare future-subjunctive form that gives the condition an old or deliberately formal style.
Sería keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds -ía to create a “would” form.
Paréntesis names the punctuation mark, while de cierre classifies it as the member of the pair that closes the expression.

cards.promptEs: «Unos dicen…; otros dicen…» y “Fire and Ice”
cards.answerEn: The wording and nine-line shape parody Robert Frost's poem “Fire and Ice,” which opens by contrasting two claims about how the world will end.
cards.noteEn: The comic replaces Frost's fire and ice with programming languages while preserving the recognizable repeated opening and much of the poem's compact form.

cards.promptEs: PERL, LISP y un paréntesis de cierre
cards.answerEn: Perl and Lisp are programming languages; Lisp represents code with many nested expressions enclosed in paired parentheses.
cards.noteEn: The comic imagines the universe as source code. The huge ) at its right edge acts like the final closing parenthesis of a Lisp program; an unmatched parenthesis can change or break the program's structure.

cards.answerEn: must; is probably (an inference, not an obligation)
cards.noteEn: Debe is a form of deber. In deber de followed by an unchanged action verb, it presents a conclusion or likely guess rather than saying that someone has a duty.

example.en: He must be busy.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something must be true because the evidence makes it likely?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern makes an inference or educated guess. Without de, deber plus an action verb more often expresses a duty or what someone should do.

example.en: They must be at home.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks an inference after deber
cards.noteEn: In deber de plus an action verb, de helps mark a guess or conclusion about what is likely true.

example.en: She must be tired.

cards.answerEn: to be (in a state or condition)
cards.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used for states, conditions, and locations. After another conjugated verb, estar itself remains unchanged.

example.en: I want to be calm.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce something that has become true and matters now?
cards.answerEn: Use ahora que, then state the situation.
cards.noteEn: Ahora means “now,” and que links it to a complete situation. The situation after que uses an ordinary verb form when the speaker presents it as a fact.

example.es: Ahora que tenemos tiempo, podemos hablar.
example.en: Now that we have time, we can talk.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes ahora que, “now that”
cards.noteEn: After ahora, que introduces the situation that is now true. It is written without an accent because it is a linking word, not the question word qué.

example.es: Ahora que estás aquí, podemos salir.
example.en: Now that you are here, we can leave.

cards.answerEn: I noticed; I became aware of
cards.noteEn: Advertí is a completed-past form of advertir. Advertir can mean either “to notice” or “to warn”; this card teaches the notice sense.

example.en: I noticed the error too late.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

example.en: I see Marta.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

example.en: I know Marta.

cards.promptEs: preposición + el que / la que / los que / las que
cards.questionEn: How do you say “the one who” or “the ones who” after a short linking word such as a or con?
cards.answerEn: Use el que, la que, los que, or las que to match the person or thing you mean.
cards.noteEn: Que introduces the description, while the article identifies the unnamed person or thing. When a comes before el que, a + el contracts to al, producing al que.

example.es: Hablo con la que llegó primero.
example.en: I am speaking with the one who arrived first.

cards.answerEn: those; the ones (as part of los que)
cards.noteEn: Los normally means “the” before a masculine plural noun. In los que followed by a description, the noun is left unstated and los identifies a masculine or mixed group: los que llegaron means “those who arrived.”

example.es: Conozco a los que viven aquí.
example.en: I know those who live here.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Unaccented mas is an old-fashioned or literary alternative to pero. Do not confuse it with más, written with an accent, which means “more” or “most.”

example.en: I wanted to help, but I could not.

cards.answerEn: Spanish puts that second verb in a special form called the subjunctive.
cards.noteEn: The first part expresses someone’s feeling or reaction. Que means “that” and introduces what they are reacting to. When the part after que has its own doer, Spanish normally changes its verb to the subjunctive: estás becomes estés in the example. English does not need a separate word for this change.
cards.questionEn: What happens to the second verb after phrases such as “I’m glad that…” or “It bothers me that…”?

example.en: I am glad that you are here.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: El hombre can refer collectively to humanity in older or literary language. La humanidad is a more explicitly inclusive choice in modern neutral prose.

example.es: La humanidad ha observado las estrellas durante siglos.
example.en: Humankind has observed the stars for centuries.

cards.noteEn: Venere is a special form of venerar, “to worship” or “to revere.” After an expression of fear followed by que, Spanish uses this form to present the feared event rather than state it as a fact.

example.es: Temo que la gente venere al líder.
example.en: I fear that people may revere the leader.

cards.promptEs: si + futuro de subjuntivo en -re (forma rara)
cards.questionEn: What does an old-fashioned verb form ending in -re mean after si?
cards.answerEn: It presents a possible future event in a rare old, legal, or deliberately formal style.
cards.noteEn: This form is called the future subjunctive: a special verb form for a future possibility. Forms include llegare, llegares, llegare, llegáremos, llegareis, and llegaren. Modern everyday Spanish normally uses the ordinary present after si instead: Si alguien llega... rather than Si alguien llegare....

example.es: Si alguien incumpliere la norma, pagará una multa.
example.en: If anyone violates the rule, they will pay a fine.

cards.answerEn: some; any (as part of alguna vez)
cards.noteEn: Alguna is the feminine singular form of alguno. With vez, it helps form alguna vez. Questions and conditions often use it for “ever,” while positive statements can use it for “sometime.”

example.en: Have you ever been here?

cards.questionEn: How do you say “ever” or “at some unspecified time”?
cards.noteEn: In questions and conditions, alguna vez often means “ever.” In a positive statement, it can mean “sometime” or “on some occasion.”

example.en: Have you ever visited Seville?

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.answerEn: (if) I should rewrite; (if) I were ever to rewrite (rare, old-fashioned form)
cards.noteEn: Reescribiere is a future-subjunctive form of reescribir, “to rewrite.” This special -re form is nearly absent from everyday Spanish but still appears in old writing, legal language, and deliberate imitation of those styles.

example.es: Si alguien reescribiere el contrato, deberá avisarnos.
example.en: If anyone should rewrite the contract, they must notify us.

cards.noteEn: Sería is the “would” form of ser, “to be.” Spanish keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds -ía.

example.en: It would be a good solution.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

example.en: We would travel by train.

cards.questionEn: What is the Spanish term for a closing parenthesis?
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses de followed by the noun cierre to identify the parenthesis that closes a pair. The opposite term is paréntesis de apertura, “opening parenthesis.”

example.en: A closing parenthesis is missing.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

example.en: I bought a history book.

cards.answerEn: closing; close (as part of paréntesis de cierre)
cards.noteEn: Cierre is a noun meaning a closing or close. After de, it can classify something by its closing function, as in paréntesis de cierre.

example.en: Look for the closing symbol.
